content_voiceover: This donut chart breaks down what actually drives Ph-like ALL at the molecular level, since it's not one lesion but a whole family of kinase-activating events that converge on similar downstream signaling. The single largest group, roughly half of cases, is CRLF2 deregulation, through IGH-CRLF2 or P2RY8-CRLF2 rearrangements or activating CRLF2 point mutations. ABL-class fusions make up about twelve percent, involving ABL1, ABL2, CSF1R, or PDGFRB, and these are important clinically because they can respond to ABL-directed tyrosine kinase inhibitors like imatinib or dasatinib. JAK2 fusions account for about seven percent, and truncating EPOR rearrangements make up another three to ten percent, both of which activate JAK-STAT signaling and may respond to JAK inhibitors. Beyond that, there's a long tail of rarer kinase abnormalities, FLT3, NTRK3, BLNK, TYK2, and PTK2B, plus additional JAK-STAT pathway mutations and Ras pathway lesions involving NRAS, KRAS, PTPN11, and NF1. The clinical takeaway is that Ph-like ALL is genomically heterogeneous, so comprehensive fusion and mutation testing, not just a single marker, is needed to identify the specific targetable lesion in each patient.
keypoints: CRLF2 deregulation (IGH/P2RY8-CRLF2, mutations) is ~50% of Ph-like ALL
keypoint_voiceover: Half of Ph-like ALL is driven by CRLF2 deregulation, so that's the single most important lesion to test for. The rest splits among ABL-class fusions, which are TKI-targetable, JAK2 fusions and EPOR rearrangements feeding JAK-STAT signaling, and a smaller Ras-pathway mutant group. Comprehensive genomic testing is required since no single assay catches them all.
